blocks.title: Watch: Ted and Rupert play darts
Episode and scene cue
blocks.body:
Season 1 · Episode 8 · The Diamond Dogs

Start with Rupert challenging Ted in the pub. Include Ted explaining the assumptions people make about him and the final throws.

blocks.title: Before you watch
blocks.body: What did Rupert assume, and what could one sincere question have revealed?

blocks.title: Ted and Rupert’s darts match · The Best Movie Clips on the Planet
blocks.caption: scene · Watch the questions Rupert never asks and the assumptions he makes about Ted. · Start: 0s

blocks.title: Understand the scene
blocks.body: Rupert treats Ted as an easy opponent and uses their darts game to try to embarrass him. Ted calmly reveals that he has played for years. Rupert has judged Ted's appearance and manner without asking about his experience. Ted wins the game and explains the value of curiosity.

items.title: Ted notices an assumption without accepting it as truth.
He stays composed while Rupert tries to provoke him.
He connects the encounter to the questions people fail to ask.

blocks.title: Why this represents leadership
blocks.body: Leaders make poor decisions when a first impression becomes a verdict. Curiosity creates a pause in which missing information can surface. That pause can uncover a person's experience, the constraints behind a delay, or an explanation for an unfamiliar approach. The transferable behavior is inquiry before evaluation. Winning an argument is less useful than improving the quality of the judgment that follows.

blocks.title: Apply it at work
blocks.body: A new analyst is quiet in meetings, so a manager assumes she lacks initiative. In a one-to-one conversation, the manager learns that she is testing a serious data-quality concern and does not want to make an unsupported claim. Asking first changes both the assessment and the support she needs.

items.title: Name your initial assumption privately.
Ask an open question about experience, reasoning, or constraints.
Compare the answer with evidence before deciding.

blocks.body: Walk me through what you are seeing that I may be missing.

blocks.title: Use judgment
blocks.body: Curiosity does not remove the need to evaluate performance. Ask, verify, then act. Do not use a dramatic public reveal to humiliate someone who made an assumption.

blocks.title: What improvement might look like
blocks.body: Better-informed decisions and fewer misplaced judgments are possible. Track how often new information changes your first assessment.

blocks.title: Who have you recently assessed from limited information?

blocks.title: Understand the scene
blocks.body: When Ted arrives at Richmond, he meets Nate, the kit man. Ted asks his name and engages with him as a person. Nate is surprised that the new head coach wants to know who he is. A small interaction establishes that status will not determine who receives Ted's attention.

items.title: Ted asks for and uses Nate's name.
He gives a support role direct attention.
He treats an introduction as a human connection, not a hierarchy check.

blocks.title: Why this represents leadership
blocks.body: People learn their standing through everyday encounters. When leaders acknowledge only senior or visible employees, they signal whose knowledge and effort count. Respect across roles makes it easier for overlooked colleagues to contribute and raise concerns. The competency is expressed in ordinary conduct: attention, courtesy, inclusion, and fair treatment. A warm greeting matters most when it is followed by equitable access and decisions.

blocks.title: Apply it at work
blocks.body: A hospital department leader includes reception, cleaning, and scheduling colleagues in a discussion about patient delays. Their observations reveal handoff problems the clinical leaders have not seen. The leader learns names, invites their input, and reports back on changes instead of treating their work as background support.

items.title: Learn the names and responsibilities of people outside your usual circle.
Invite input from those closest to the work.
Apply the same courtesy and response standards across roles.

blocks.body: You see this part of the operation every day. What should we understand?

blocks.title: Use judgment
blocks.body: Do not confuse friendliness with fairness. Examine whose ideas receive time, whose work receives credit, and who gets development opportunities.

blocks.title: What improvement might look like
blocks.body: More useful operational information and stronger participation may follow. Check whether contributions and opportunities reach people at every level.

blocks.title: Before you watch
blocks.body: Which part builds credibility: the gift, the attention, or the repeated follow-through?

blocks.title: Biscuits with the boss · Coach Lasso

blocks.title: Understand the scene
blocks.body: Ted brings Rebecca a box of biscuits and tries to establish a regular conversation with her. She is guarded and does not immediately welcome his approach. Ted continues showing up. The biscuits become a recurring relationship ritual rather than a single attempt to win her approval.

items.title: Ted makes time for contact beyond immediate tasks.
He repeats a small, dependable action.
He remains patient when the relationship is initially distant.

blocks.title: Why this represents leadership
blocks.body: Trust needs evidence over time. Reliable actions reduce uncertainty about whether a leader will listen, keep a promise, or remain available under pressure. A repeated ritual can provide that evidence, but it must serve the other person rather than the leader's desire to be liked. In an organization, honoring a commitment is usually more powerful than a memorable gesture.

blocks.title: Apply it at work
blocks.body: After a reorganization, a supervisor holds a short weekly check-in, answers questions honestly, and records what she promises to investigate. At the next meeting, she closes each loop, including explaining what she could not change. Predictable follow-through gradually makes the meetings credible.

items.title: Choose one useful commitment you can sustain.
Agree on a rhythm that works for the other person.
Follow up on promises, including delays and limits.

blocks.body: I said I would check on this. Here is what I learned, and here is the next step.

blocks.title: Use judgment
blocks.body: Respect people's time and preferences. Gifts, persistent visits, and personal rituals are not appropriate in every relationship. Consistency should never override a boundary.

blocks.title: What improvement might look like
blocks.body: More predictable communication and greater confidence in commitments may follow. Measure whether promised follow-ups happen when agreed.

blocks.title: Watch: Roy supports Jamie after his father's abuse
Episode and scene cue
blocks.body:
Season 2 · Episode 8 · Man City

Find the locker-room confrontation after the Manchester City loss. Include the moment Jamie's father leaves and Roy approaches Jamie.

blocks.title: Before you watch
blocks.body: How does Roy recognize what Jamie needs without turning the moment into a speech?

blocks.title: Roy supports Jamie after his father’s outburst · Crusey1988
blocks.caption: scene · The clip includes the locker-room confrontation and Roy’s hug. Notice how Roy responds without demanding an explanation. · Start: 0s

blocks.title: Understand the scene
blocks.body: After Richmond's heavy loss, Jamie's father enters the locker room and humiliates him. The confrontation escalates before his father is removed. Jamie stands shaken in front of his teammates. Roy approaches and embraces him, setting their usual antagonism aside to offer support at a vulnerable moment.

items.title: Roy notices distress beneath Jamie's usual confident presentation.
He responds to the person rather than continuing their rivalry.
He offers presence before analysis or criticism.

blocks.title: Why this represents leadership
blocks.body: Empathy means noticing another person's experience and responding usefully. It helps a leader distinguish a coaching need from a moment that calls for care. When someone is overwhelmed, immediate critique may prevent them from processing either the event or the feedback. Support can create the conditions for a later performance conversation. It does not require sharing the same experience or excusing harmful behavior.

blocks.title: Apply it at work
blocks.body: A team member returns from a difficult customer interaction visibly upset. Her manager first offers a private pause and asks what support she wants. Once she is ready, they review the interaction and identify any training or escalation changes. Care and learning happen in an appropriate order.

items.title: Notice changes in tone, posture, or participation.
Offer support and ask what would help.
Return to work decisions when the person can engage.

blocks.body: That looked difficult. Would you like some space, someone to listen, or help with the next step?

blocks.title: Use judgment
blocks.body: Do not assume physical contact is welcome. Ask or use another form of support. Protect the person from public probing and address threatening conduct through appropriate channels.

blocks.title: What improvement might look like
blocks.body: People may recover and re-engage more readily. Look for whether support leads to a useful follow-up rather than avoiding the work issue.

blocks.title: Watch: The team responds when Colin comes out
Episode and scene cue
blocks.body:
Season 3 · Episode 9 · La Locker Room Aux Folles

Find Colin speaking to the team at halftime, followed by Ted's response. Keep enough of the conversation to see the difference between indifference and support.

blocks.title: Before you watch
blocks.body: What makes a response communicate that a teammate matters, rather than that his identity is irrelevant?

blocks.title: Ted responds to Colin · Apple TV
blocks.caption: excerpt · Official excerpt of Ted’s response. Colin’s initial disclosure and the wider team conversation come from the full episode. · Start: 0s

blocks.title: Understand the scene
blocks.body: Colin tells his teammates that he is gay. As the team responds, Ted explains that simply saying they do not care is not the whole message they need to convey. He reframes the response around caring about Colin and supporting him through what he has been carrying alone.

items.title: The team listens to Colin's disclosure.
Ted distinguishes acceptance from indifference.
He makes support for the person an explicit team responsibility.

blocks.title: Why this represents leadership
blocks.body: Belonging is stronger when people can participate without hiding important parts of themselves. A neutral response may sound accepting while leaving someone unsure whether support will be available when it costs something. Leaders make inclusion credible by responding to exclusion, applying fair standards, and respecting individual choice. The point is to affirm a person's place on the team, not to make them represent an entire group.

blocks.title: Apply it at work
blocks.body: An employee describes being excluded from client-facing opportunities after sharing a personal identity. The leader thanks him for raising it, asks what support he wants, examines assignment decisions, and addresses the exclusion. The response moves from an inclusive statement to a fair change in practice.

items.title: Acknowledge the trust involved in sharing.
Ask what support and privacy the person wants.
Address barriers in assignments, behavior, and team norms.

blocks.body: You belong on this team. What would meaningful support look like for you?

blocks.title: Use judgment
blocks.body: Disclosure must be voluntary. Do not ask colleagues to reveal identities, tell their story publicly, or reassure the rest of the team. Follow their lead on privacy.

blocks.title: What improvement might look like
blocks.body: Participation and trust may improve when support becomes tangible. Review access to opportunities and how quickly exclusion is addressed.

blocks.title: Watch: The coaches admit what they have been hiding
Episode and scene cue
blocks.body:
Season 2 · Episode 8 · Man City

Find the coaches' private conversation in which Ted explains why he left the Tottenham match. Include the other coaches' admissions.

blocks.title: Before you watch
blocks.body: What makes an honest admission easier, and what responsibilities follow once someone shares it?

blocks.title: Video slot
blocks.body: An exact YouTube clip of the coaches’ private admissions before the Wembley match was not found.

blocks.title: Understand the scene
blocks.body: Ted tells the other coaches that a panic attack, rather than the explanation previously given, caused him to leave a match. Others also admit things they have concealed or mishandled. The conversation briefly makes it possible to stop protecting an image of infallibility and speak more honestly.

items.title: Ted corrects an incomplete account of what happened.
He admits vulnerability before asking it of others.
The coaches make room for additional admissions.

blocks.title: Why this represents leadership
blocks.body: A leader's response to uncomfortable information teaches people what is safe to report. If every admission brings humiliation, problems travel underground. Candor helps teams detect mistakes, risks, and support needs earlier. This scene also has an important limit: Nate later discloses Ted's private information to the press. A receptive conversation alone cannot guarantee safety. Confidentiality, fair responses, and accountability must support it.

blocks.title: Apply it at work
blocks.body: At a project review, a director acknowledges that her own estimate was unrealistic. She invites the team to identify overlooked risks, thanks them for specifics, and assigns corrective actions. She does not punish someone for surfacing a concern or allow personal disclosures to become meeting gossip.

items.title: Model a relevant admission without demanding personal disclosure.
Thank people for raising risks and clarify the facts.
Agree on privacy, corrective action, and fair accountability.

blocks.body: Thank you for telling us early. What happened, and what should we change now?

blocks.title: Use judgment
blocks.body: Honesty is not immunity from standards. Separate good-faith reporting from intentional harm, and keep health information within the boundaries the person chooses.

blocks.title: What improvement might look like
blocks.body: Earlier reporting can reduce avoidable surprises. Track the time between a problem being noticed and being raised, alongside the response it receives.

lessons.title: Listen before trying to fix things

blocks.title: Watch: Roy speaks with the Diamond Dogs
Episode and scene cue
blocks.body:
Season 2 · Episode 12 · Inverting the Pyramid of Success

Find Roy describing his feelings about Keeley's magazine photographs. Include his realization that the group can talk without solving everything.

blocks.title: Before you watch
blocks.body: Where does the conversation provide space rather than a solution?

blocks.title: Video slot
blocks.body: An exact YouTube clip of Roy discovering that the Diamond Dogs can listen without solving his problem was not found.

blocks.title: Understand the scene
blocks.body: Roy joins the coaches' discussion to talk about feeling left out of Keeley's magazine feature and about their relationship. Near the end, he realizes that the Diamond Dogs can sometimes simply talk: nobody has to solve the problem or make something change. He finds value in that possibility.

items.title: Roy puts a difficult feeling into words.
The group allows a conversation without a forced resolution.
He recognizes that being heard can itself be useful.

blocks.title: Why this represents leadership
blocks.body: Leaders often move quickly from a concern to a solution. That can solve the wrong problem or make the speaker feel dismissed. Listening first helps clarify whether the person needs space, perspective, a decision, or practical help. It also preserves their ownership of the next step. Listening becomes a leadership skill when attention and accurate understanding guide the eventual response.

blocks.title: Apply it at work
blocks.body: A colleague is frustrated after a presentation. Before rewriting her slides, the supervisor asks whether she wants to talk through the experience or receive feedback. She first needs to process a difficult exchange; later, she asks for help preparing a better answer to the client's question.

items.title: Ask whether the person wants listening, advice, or action.
Summarize what you heard and check your understanding.
Offer next steps only when they fit the need.

blocks.body: Would it help most if I listened, helped you think it through, or worked on a solution with you?

blocks.title: Use judgment
blocks.body: A work hazard or urgent decision may require action even while you listen. Do not use listening as a reason to avoid a responsibility that belongs to you.

blocks.title: What improvement might look like
blocks.body: Fewer misdirected fixes and clearer conversations may follow. Check whether the person agrees that you understood the issue before proposing a response.

blocks.title: Watch: Ted asks Roy to help Isaac
Episode and scene cue
blocks.body:
Season 2 · Episode 5 · Rainbow

Find Ted asking Roy for help with Isaac's difficulty as captain. Pair it with Roy taking Isaac to the neighborhood pitch if useful.

blocks.title: Before you watch
blocks.body: How does Ted remain responsible while admitting that another person may be better placed to help?

blocks.title: Video slot
blocks.body: An exact YouTube clip of Ted asking Roy to help Isaac at the kebab shop was not found.

blocks.title: Understand the scene
blocks.body: Isaac is struggling with the pressure of being captain. Ted asks Roy to help him, recognizing that Roy's experience and relationship with the players offer something Ted cannot supply alone. Roy takes Isaac back to a local football setting and helps him reconnect with the game.

items.title: Ted recognizes a limit in his own experience.
He asks a person with relevant credibility for help.
He leaves room for Roy to use a different approach.

blocks.title: Why this represents leadership
blocks.body: Humility lets a leader separate responsibility from the need to have every answer. Asking for help can improve a decision and model learning for the team. It also gives expertise room to operate. The leader still defines the need and follows through; admitting a limit is not the same as abandoning the problem. Competence includes knowing when another person has a better perspective.

blocks.title: Apply it at work
blocks.body: A manager cannot resolve a recurring conflict between two technical teams. She invites an experienced project lead to facilitate a conversation, explains the desired outcome, and supports the agreements they reach. She does not pretend that positional authority makes her the best facilitator.

items.title: Name the problem and the limit of your current approach.
Ask for help based on relevant experience.
Support the contributor and remain accountable for follow-through.

blocks.body: I have not found the right approach. Your experience could help us see this differently.

blocks.title: Use judgment
blocks.body: Give a helper context, authority, and time. Do not hand off a difficult issue without support or treat asking for help as a performance confession.

blocks.title: What improvement might look like
blocks.body: Better use of available experience may improve problem solving. Track whether help seeking produces an agreed next step and resolves the underlying issue.

blocks.title: Understand the scene

items.title: Ted gives an unexpected contributor room to explain.
The coaches assess the idea rather than the job title.

blocks.title: Why this represents leadership
blocks.body: Knowledge is distributed across an organization. People who observe the work closely may notice options that formal experts miss. This lesson differs from respect alone: a contribution has influence over the actual work. The leader creates a route from insight to a decision.

blocks.title: Apply it at work
blocks.body: A warehouse assistant notices that a packaging change would remove a repeated handoff. The operations leader asks him to explain, checks the safety and cost implications with specialists, and runs a limited trial. The suggestion receives a reasoned decision and a response, rather than disappearing into a suggestion box.

items.title: Ask people close to the work what they notice.
Evaluate suggestions against clear criteria.
Test a promising idea and report what happened.

Episode and scene cue

Find Beard confronting Ted about his reluctance to make a difficult selection decision involving Roy. Include the disagreement about results.

blocks.title: Before you watch
blocks.body: What important consideration does Beard put back into a conversation dominated by Ted's concern for Roy?

blocks.title: Video slot
blocks.body: An exact YouTube clip of Beard challenging Ted about winning and Roy’s selection in the pub was not found.

blocks.title: Understand the scene
blocks.body: Ted struggles with the prospect of leaving Roy out of the starting lineup. Beard pushes back on Ted's tendency to downplay winning, pointing out the importance of results in professional sport. A trusted colleague challenges the head coach rather than simply reinforcing his preferred perspective.

items.title: Beard raises a disagreement about a consequential decision.
He connects the challenge to the team's responsibilities.
Ted has to consider a perspective that complicates his own.

blocks.title: Why this represents leadership
blocks.body: A team becomes less capable when agreement is the price of belonging. Constructive challenge can reveal tradeoffs a leader is minimizing: performance, fairness, cost, or impact on other people. The purpose is a better decision, not proving the leader wrong. Welcoming challenge requires space before the decision, a reasoned response, and protection from retaliation afterward.

blocks.title: Apply it at work
blocks.body: A director wants to keep extending a struggling pilot because the team worked hard on it. Her deputy points to missed targets and the effect on other services. They agree on a final evidence threshold and a decision date. Respect for the team's effort remains, while the decision becomes more disciplined.

items.title: Invite the strongest case against your preferred option.
Ask for evidence and consequences, not just opinions.
Explain how the challenge affected the final decision.

blocks.body: What am I giving too little weight to in this decision?

blocks.title: Use judgment
blocks.body: Beard's delivery is heated. In a workplace, challenge the reasoning directly while avoiding contempt, personal attacks, or public humiliation.

blocks.body: Better-balanced decisions and earlier detection of weak plans may follow. Check whether dissent changes decisions and whether challengers remain included.

blocks.title: Watch: Nate is promoted to assistant coach
Episode and scene cue

Find Nate discovering a new kit man and initially fearing he has been replaced. Include the reveal that he is becoming an assistant coach.

blocks.title: Before you watch
blocks.body: What earlier evidence makes this opportunity more than a reassuring compliment?

blocks.title: Nate’s promotion to coach · naveen kumar
blocks.caption: scene · Watch Nate’s changing interpretation of the new kit man, the whistle, and the team’s response. · Start: 0s

blocks.title: Understand the scene
blocks.body: Nate finds someone else doing his kit-man work and fears that he is losing his place at Richmond. Ted and the coaches explain that he has been promoted to assistant coach. His contributions have led to a real change in responsibility, turning recognition of potential into an opportunity to grow.

items.title: The coaches notice capability beyond Nate's existing role.
They connect his contribution to a development opportunity.
They give him a place in the coaching team.

blocks.title: Why this represents leadership
blocks.body: Belief becomes useful when it creates access to practice, responsibility, and support. People can be trapped by their current title even after showing readiness for more. A leader should notice evidence of potential and offer a fair route to develop it. Nate's later difficulties also show that promotion is a beginning: growing authority requires ongoing feedback and expectations about how others are treated.

blocks.title: Apply it at work
blocks.body: A coordinator repeatedly improves team scheduling. Her manager invites her to lead a limited planning cycle, provides a mentor, and agrees on success criteria before considering a broader role. The opportunity is based on demonstrated contributions, and other employees can see how to qualify for similar development.

items.title: Identify a specific contribution that indicates readiness.
Offer a meaningful stretch with support.
Review both results and treatment of others.

blocks.body: Your work on this suggests you are ready to try a larger responsibility. Let's agree on the support you will need.

blocks.body: Do not substitute favoritism or enthusiasm for fair selection. Explain criteria, provide support, and monitor how new authority is used.

blocks.title: Watch: Roy gives Jamie a signal to use his competitive edge
Episode and scene cue

Find Roy explaining what has changed in Jamie's play, then the sideline signal that gives Jamie permission to use his assertiveness.

blocks.title: Before you watch
blocks.body: How does Roy distinguish a useful strength from the way that strength can harm the team?

blocks.title: Roy coaches Jamie’s assertiveness · Warner Bros. TV
blocks.caption: scene · Official compilation cued to Roy’s coaching and the on-field signal. Focus on the skill Jamie needs to use at the right time. · Start: 78s · Pause at 294s

blocks.title: Understand the scene
blocks.body: Jamie has become more cooperative but is struggling to use the confidence that once drove his play. Roy coaches him to bring back his competitive edge at the right moment, with a signal from the sideline. The instruction responds to Jamie's particular needs rather than giving every player the same message.

items.title: Roy identifies a specific strength Jamie has suppressed.
He ties its use to the team's situation.
He creates a clear cue for applying the coaching.

blocks.title: Why this represents leadership
blocks.body: People can need different support to meet the same standard. One colleague may need encouragement to speak; another may need help making room for others. blocks.title: Why this represents leadership
blocks.body: A leader's emotional state can affect attention, patience, and decisions. Self-management includes recognizing strain and arranging support, rather than maintaining a convincing appearance at all costs. blocks.body: A director notices that sustained pressure is making her reactive in meetings. blocks.title: Why this represents leadership

Boundaries allow support without making private matters part of someone's workplace identity against their wishes. The same principle applies to family circumstances, health, and sensitive aspirations.

blocks.body: An employee privately explains a family difficulty that affects availability. The manager agrees on scheduling changes and asks what, if anything, should be shared with the team. Colleagues receive the information needed for coverage, while the personal details remain private.

blocks.body: A design team has become exhausted by constant approval reviews. Its leader protects a short session to solve a real customer problem together without presentation scoring. blocks.title: Why this represents leadership
blocks.body: Leadership is more durable when decisions, relationships, and capability are shared. A team that can function only through one person is exposed whenever that person is absent or leaves. Developing others requires delegated authority, practice, feedback, and access to information. Succession is evidence that the organization can continue serving its purpose. A leader's influence can remain useful without requiring their permanent presence.

blocks.title: Apply it at work
blocks.body: A department head preparing for a new role gradually transfers decisions to capable colleagues, records essential processes, and creates opportunities for them to lead meetings and stakeholder conversations. She tests the handover during an absence and fixes gaps before leaving rather than relying on a farewell presentation.

Test continuity while you are absent and close the gaps.
